Interconnectors

Ten subsea and tunnel cables connect Great Britain to six countries. This is what each one is doing right now, and what decides which way it runs.

Interconnector flows

INTOUTHH · half-hourly
24h 7d
Import into GB (+) Export from GB (−) Capacity, both directions

Net position = Imports − Exports • All flows are physical energy in the last 30 minutes.

How to read the panel

Each row is one cable. The bar runs from a shared centre line: right and teal is energy arriving in GB, left and dark red is energy leaving it. The pale track behind the bar is that link's capacity in both directions, so the bar's share of the track is the share of the cable actually in use — which is why two links carrying very different megawatts can show bars of similar length.

Net position at the top is imports minus exports across all ten links: one number for whether GB is drawing on its neighbours or supplying them. A link sitting at zero is idle and counted in neither total.

What decides which way the power flows

Almost always, price. Power moves from the cheaper market to the dearer one, and the trader moving it keeps the difference. When GB prices are high — a still, cold evening — the links fill with imports; when GB wind is abundant and prices fall, the flows reverse. That is why the interconnector panel and the wind panel so often move together.

How that trade is arranged changed with Brexit, and the change is visible in the data. Before 2021 GB was part of the EU's Single Day-Ahead Coupling, where an algorithm set cross-border flows and prices together and capacity was allocated implicitly — buy the power, get the cable. GB now sits outside that arrangement, so capacity on most links is allocated explicitly: traders buy the right to use a cable in an auction, then separately buy the power, then nominate the flow.

⚠ One consequence is worth knowing, because it shows up as apparently irrational flows. Day-ahead capacity auctions on explicitly allocated links close before the day-ahead power markets they serve. A trader is therefore betting on tomorrow's price spread rather than responding to it — so a cable can run the "wrong" way, or sit part-empty while prices diverge, without anything being broken.

Two links are exceptions and behave differently for that reason. Capacity to Ireland is allocated through simultaneous intraday auctions, and capacity to Norway follows the Nord Pool day-ahead auction — so both track price more closely, and the Irish links in particular can reverse more abruptly than the continental ones.

Why a link can read more than 100% of capacity

It happens regularly on this page, and it is not an error in the feed or in the figure above it. The percentage compares the metered flow against the link's nameplate capacity — the headline rating the cable was built to. Three things put a real flow above it:

  • Short-term uprates. Operators run cables above nameplate when conditions allow. NESO's own status reports have listed Viking Link at 1,450 MW against a 1,400 MW rating.
  • Nameplate is a round number. Nemo Link is sold as 1,000 MW and rated at 1,012 MW; several links have been uprated since commissioning without the headline figure changing.
  • The measurement point. The flow is metered at the GB boundary, and a cable loses energy along its length — so the figure at one end is not the figure at the other.

The opposite case matters more, and only one link states it plainly: Moyle's 500 MW is a technical rating, and its firm export capacity is considerably lower. A bar filling half that track may already be at the commercial limit. Where an operator publishes such a limit, this dashboard says so on the link's own detail.

The ten links

Great Britain has 10 electricity interconnectors to six countries, 10.3 GW of capacity in total. All are HVDC — direct current, with a converter station at each end — because alternating current cannot be run over these distances subsea. Nine are submarine cables; ElecLink is the exception, running through the Channel Tunnel.

Capacity is nameplate rating. A dash means the operator does not publish that detail — it is left blank rather than filled from a secondary source, which is the same rule the link tooltips follow. Click any link in the panel above for its full detail and the operator's own page.

What this data cannot see

  • These are settlement-period values, not live meter readings. Elexon publishes INTOUTHH per half-hour settlement period, so an interconnector figure can lag the five-minute fuel mix by up to thirty minutes. The two panels on the dashboard are not disagreeing when they differ — they are describing different instants.
  • Physical flow, not contracted position. What is shown is energy that moved. Traders' positions, capacity holdings and nominations are separate, and a link can be fully sold while flowing well below its capacity.
  • Capacities are held here, not fetched. No key-free public endpoint publishes interconnector capacity, so the ten figures are recorded values with the date they were last verified. They are what the percentage and the capacity track are computed from.
  • Northern Ireland is a separate system. Moyle connects GB to the all-island Irish market rather than to another GB region, which is why it appears here alongside the international links.

Where these figures come from

Flows are Elexon Insights INTOUTHH, the half-hourly interconnector outturn used in settlement. Link detail — capacity, route, converter technology and ownership — is compiled from each operator's own published material and from NESO, Elexon and public network registers. How the flows enter every other figure on this site is set out on the Methodology page; the licences the data carries are on the About page.
